name: Uma Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This is Hillcrest Farm, and my great-grandfather cleared the top fields by hand. Daniel and I run it with two part-timers: 90 dairy cows, 250 ewes, hay and spring barley on 140 hectares. I'm in the parlour at five, Daniel does the young stock, and after breakfast with the kids it's whatever the day throws at us. Sundays we milk, go to chapel, and milk again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love walking the cows in on a June morning with the mist still on the river. I love that my children know the name of every field, the same names my grandmother used. What wears me down is the milk price, and the dairy company that buys our milk sending new rules every year about records and apps. And the loan, because when Dad died we borrowed to buy out my two brothers' shares so the farm stayed whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could have told them that, it's a lot of noise about a gadget. At chapel and at the market I'd say good, now maybe they'll leave farmers alone to farm. I don't do anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch my real worries. The milk price is set by the dairy company, and they pay what they like. The loan on the farm takes a big bite every quarter, and the bank doesn't care whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are, milking, lambing, making hay. I'd keep a closer eye on spending, because the milk price dropped twice last year. Daniel would keep doing his hedge-cutting for neighbours in the winter, which pays the feed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same as always. Farming is never comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the milk price dropped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second part-timer, Ruth, which would break my heart because she's been with us eight years. Before that we'd stop the kids' riding lessons and put off fixing the barn roof. We never cut the cows' feed, ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you turn to when things get hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My brother Peter would lend a hand at silage time without being asked, and chapel folk would bring a meal. We look after our own here, we don't wait for government.

say: I'd say it's a lot of **noise about a gadget**.
At **chapel and market** I'd say good, maybe they'll leave farmers alone now.
think: The **dairy company** sets the milk price, and that's the real worry.
The **farm loan** from buying out my brothers takes a big bite every quarter.
do: **Carry on** milking, lambing and making hay as we do.
Keep a **closer eye on spending** after last year's price drops.
Keep Daniel's **winter hedge-cutting** going to pay the feed bill.
feel: **Uneasy**, as always, because farming is never comfortable.
S0.quote: We never cut the cows' feed, ever.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **milk price** and the buyout loan, not AI.
Strong sense of **duty** to the family land.
Relies on **family and chapel**, not government, when things get hard.
Would cut **Ruth's hours** last, but would if forced.

steps.text: Keep milking 90 cows and lambing 250 ewes as now
Stop the kids' riding lessons if the milk price drops again
Keep Daniel's winter hedge-cutting to cover the feed bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the city jobs that'll feel it, and good luck to them. But I'd also say leave farming alone, we don't need a computer telling us when to cut hay. At the farmers' union meeting I'd say we should fight the dairy company's data rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the dairy company would use AI to plan collections and set prices, and they'd want every farm on their app. The big farms with robot milkers would grow and get the better price. Small family farms like Hillcrest would get squeezed, slowly, and I don't know how long we'd hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse to use the app until I absolutely had to, and I'd ask our union rep to fight the rules. We'd cut back on anything that isn't the farm. And I'd wait and see what the neighbours do before I spend money on anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. And cross, because it's being done to us, not by us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said small farms get squeezed slowly. What does that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeezed slowly looks like the milk lorry coming every other day, because Hillcrest is too small to bother with. It looks like a price letter every spring that's a little worse. And one day Daniel saying we should sell the cows and keep the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace and Samuel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the farm is theirs if they want it, and that we'll fight for it. Samuel's ten and already says he's going to be a farmer. I'd want him to have a farm to come home to.

say: I'd say leave farming alone; we don't need a **computer** telling us when to cut hay.
I'd tell the union to fight the **dairy company's data rules**.
think: The dairy company would use AI to **set prices** and push everyone onto its app.
**Big robot farms** would grow and family farms like Hillcrest would be squeezed.
do: **Refuse the app** until it's absolutely required.
Ask our **union rep** to fight the new rules.
**Cut back** on anything that isn't the farm and wait on the neighbours.
feel: **Worried**, and cross that it's being done to farmers, not by them.
S1.quote: Squeezed slowly looks like the milk lorry coming every other day, because Hillcrest is too small to bother with.
fieldNote: Sees AI mainly in the **buyer's hands**, used against small farms.
**Resists** the app on principle and waits on neighbours.
Blames the **dairy company** and big farms, not the technology itself.
Her son's dream of farming raises the **stakes**.

steps.text: Refuse the dairy company's app until it's compulsory
Ask the farmers' union rep to fight the new data rules
Cut household spending that isn't the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, plain wrong, and the government that lets it happen should be thrown out. I'd say it at chapel and the market and anywhere else. People who've never farmed are going to decide we're not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the end of dairying at Hillcrest. In 2028 the dairy company runs on AI, and by 2031 the big farms have robots that milk, feed and calve. They'll produce milk so cheap that our 90 cows can't pay the loan, and the bank won't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at home that isn't food and fuel, starting this month. I'd talk to my brothers about whether the family could help with the loan if it came to it. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect family farms. And I'd start thinking about selling the dairy herd and keeping the sheep, which hurts to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said selling the herd hurts to say. What would that day be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling the dairy herd would be like a funeral, because those cows are my great-grandfather's line, bred on this farm for ninety years. Watching the lorry take them to market would be the worst day since Dad died.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your brothers. Isn't that hard, after buying them out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is hard. Peter would help, he loves the place. Michael would say I told you so. But family is family, and that's who you ask first.

say: I'd say it's **plain wrong**, and the government that allows it should go.
I'd say people who've **never farmed** will decide we're not needed.
think: By **2031** robot farms make milk so cheap our 90 cows can't pay the loan.
It would be the **end of dairying** at Hillcrest.
do: Cut everything but **food and fuel** at home this month.
Ask my **brothers** whether the family could help with the loan.
Consider **selling the dairy herd** and keeping the sheep.
S2.quote: Selling the dairy herd would be like a funeral, because those cows are my great-grandfather's line, bred on this farm for ninety years.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose dairying** and most of the farm's income.
Turns to **family first**, even the brother who'll say I told you so.
Anger aimed at **government and outsiders** who've never farmed.
The **herd's bloodline** matters to her as much as the money.

steps.text: Cut all household spending except food and fuel this month
Ask her brothers Peter and Michael for help with the farm loan
Vote for candidates who promise to protect family farms
Sell the dairy herd and keep the 250 ewes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, and somebody should put the brakes on. I'd say it at the union and at chapel. I'd say family farms feed this country and always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same ending, just later. By 2034 the robot farms are up and running, I'd be 51, Grace would be at college and Samuel 18. It gives us time to pay down more of the loan, but I can't see Hillcrest milking cows in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as we are and pay every spare bit off the loan. I'd look at selling milk direct from the farm gate, cheese maybe, because people still want proper milk from a farm they know. And I'd talk with Samuel about whether he really wants the farm. I won't hand my son a sinking ship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less frightened, but sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling direct means dealing with customers and maybe technology for orders. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would do the computer side, she's good at it. I'd make the cheese and talk to people at the gate. That's farming too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would chapel say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chapel would pray for us and bring casseroles, which helps more than you'd think. And a few of the older farmers there would buy our cheese out of loyalty. That's community.

say: I'd say **five years** is still too fast and someone should put the brakes on.
I'd say **family farms** feed this country and always have.
think: It's the **same ending, just later**: no milking at Hillcrest by 2036.
Five years lets us **pay down the loan** before the robots arrive.
do: Pay every spare amount off the **farm loan**.
Look at selling **milk and cheese** direct from the farm gate.
Talk to **Samuel** honestly about whether he wants the farm.
S3.quote: I won't hand my son a sinking ship.
fieldNote: Extra time softens fear into **sadness**, not hope.
Would sell direct, letting **Grace** handle the technology.
Community and **chapel** are her safety net.
Thinks about the farm as an **inheritance** for Samuel.

steps.text: Pay every spare amount off the farm loan
Start selling milk and cheese direct from the farm gate
Talk with Samuel about whether he really wants Hillcrest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is better, and farmers should use it to stand together. I'd say it at the union. I'd still say it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when the robots come in 2039, the loan nearly paid, the kids grown. Hillcrest might survive as a smaller farm, sheep and a few cows for cheese. It wouldn't be what it was, but it might still be ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal in the first year. I'd keep paying down the loan. And I'd wait to see what the dairy company does before I change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at best, anxious at worst. Mostly sad about the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the cows. Why does that matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because cows are what my family has done here for ninety years. Sheep are fine, but the parlour is the heart of the farm. Without it, it's a different place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Samuel still wanted to farm in ten years, what would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn whatever the robots need, so he can keep the land in the family. I don't like it, but I'd rather my son farmed with robots than sold Hillcrest to someone who does.

say: I'd say **ten years** is better than two, but it's still wrong.
I'd tell the union farmers should **stand together** and use the decade.
think: At **53** in 2039, with the loan nearly paid, Hillcrest might survive smaller.
It wouldn't be what it was, but it might **still be ours**.
do: Carry on **as normal** in the first year.
Wait to see what the **dairy company** does.
S4.quote: I'd rather my son farmed with robots than sold Hillcrest to someone who does.
fieldNote: Ten years doesn't remove her expectation of **shrinking income**.
Willing to accept **robots for her son** to keep the land.
The **parlour** is the heart of her identity.
Resistant pace: **wait** on the dairy company first.

steps.text: Carry on milking and lambing as normal this year
Keep paying down the farm loan from the buyout
Wait for the dairy company's plans before changing anything

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd lose the dairy before we'd paid the loan. What would help is a fair milk price, guaranteed for family farms, and the bank giving farmers time. Not handouts, just a fair chance to keep going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. Land isn't just a place to put machines, it's where my family is buried. Whatever robots come, I'd want the land to stay in families who love it.

headlineQuote: Land isn't just a place to put machines, it's where my family is buried.
portrait: **Uma Okafor**, 43, runs **Hillcrest Farm**, a fourth-generation dairy and sheep farm.
She never uses AI and resents the **dairy company's apps** and rules.
Her steady worries are the **milk price** and the loan from buying out her brothers.
Fast AGI **alarms** her, as she expects robot dairies to end Hillcrest's milking.
She leans on **family and chapel**, and wants the land kept in families.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the dairy would go before the farm loan was paid.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair milk price** guaranteed for family farms.
The bank giving farmers **time**, not handouts.
